activity: basic shape concepts such as circle, square, triangle and rectangle
story:
Arya went to the library with Dad. Story time was today. Miss Lena put paper on the big table. "We will make a little house," she said.

Arya picked a red paper. It was a square. It had four sides, all the same. She held it up. "Look, Dad. A square!" Dad smiled and nodded.

Miss Lena showed how to fold. Arya folded her square paper in half. She pressed the fold with her fingers. Then she opened it a tiny bit so it would stand up. "Oh!" said Arya. Now it was not a square. It was a rectangle. The paper looked like a little roof. Arya put it on the table. It stood all by itself.

Next to her, a boy named Sam frowned. His paper would not stand up. Arya watched him. He had not folded it yet. "Fold it in half," she said. "Like this." Sam folded his square edge to edge. He pressed it down. His paper stood up too. "It's tall now!" said Sam.

Miss Lena gave them triangle stickers for windows and a circle sticker for the sun. Arya put the circle sun on top. Then she gave Sam one more triangle, because he had none. Arya spun her little house around on the table. "My house can spin!" she said. Dad laughed and clapped his hands.

activity: searching for a lost favorite toy
story:
Olivier was at Grandma's house. His little blue bunny was gone. "Where did bunny go?" he said.

He looked under the table. No bunny. He looked in the big chair. No bunny. "Bunny, where are you?" he did call. Grandma said, "Maybe bunny is naughty and hiding." Olivier laughed. He looked and looked.

Then he saw a basket by his little bed. He peeked inside. There was bunny! "Found you!" said Olivier. Grandma smiled. "Let's put bunny in this basket every day," she said. "Then you will know just where he is."

The next morning, Olivier woke up. He peeked in the basket. Bunny was right there, waiting. Every day after that, bunny slept in the basket. And every day, Olivier knew just where to look. "Good morning, bunny," he said, with a big hug.

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
story:
Max put on his little blue apron. Today he would make pancakes for his family. His tummy made a happy grumble.

The teacher held up a card. "This is the recipe," she said. "It tells us what to do." Max looked at the steps. Flour, milk, egg, stir, stir, stir. One step, then the next step.

But Max was in a hurry. He poured the flour. He poured the milk. He skipped a step and did not put in the egg. The teacher cooked the pancakes on the hot pan. Max watched from his safe spot.

Flip! The pancake came out flat. Flat as a rain puddle on the floor. "Oh no," said Max. "Flat pancake!"

They read the recipe again. Step one, step two, step three. This time Max put in the egg. Stir, stir, stir.

The new pancake puffed up big and round. Mama took a bite. Papa took a bite. Max clapped his hands. "The recipe helped!" he said. "More please!"

story:

He kicked the ball. It was hard to kick far. A big kid helped him. They took turns and did not share well at first. Then they made a game of it. Soon Joshua was tired. He went back to the bench.

Bunny was not there! Joshua looked under the bench. He looked by the tree. A kind man held up Bunny. "Is this yours?" he asked. He pointed at the tag. Mommy had written Joshua on it. "It says Joshua," the man said. Joshua hugged Bunny tight. "Thank you," he said. He held Bunny with one hand and the ball with the other, all the way home.

activity: searching for a lost favorite toy
story:
Arthur rode the city bus with his mama. He held his toy bunny on his lap. Then the bus went bump, bump, bump. Arthur looked down. The bunny was gone!

Arthur ran up the aisle. He ran back down. He looked fast, fast, fast. Where could the bunny be? He peeked under one seat. Then another. But he ran so fast, his eyes missed things.

Arthur stopped. He took a big breath. "I will look one seat at a time," he said. He looked under seat one. Snow was melting off someone's boots there. He looked under seat two. Only a bit of dirt. He looked under seat three. There was his bunny, lying neat and still!

Arthur picked up the bunny and hugged it tight. "I found you," he whispered. The bus doors opened with a whoosh.

story:
Alexander wanted Grandpa to read the owl book. Grandpa picked it up. He squinted at the page. "Wait," he said. He went to the table.

Grandpa put on his glasses. Then he read the first page. His voice was big and warm. Alexander heard every word. The owl went "hoo, hoo" in the story.

Alexander wondered about the glasses. Did they help Grandpa? He wanted to find out. Grandpa put the glasses down on the couch. Alexander picked them up very carefully. He put them on his own nose.

The room looked funny. Everything looked big and blurry. Alexander laughed. "The glasses are for Grandpa," he said. He gave them back. Grandpa put them on and read the rest of the story. Alexander touched the soft book page. He smelled popcorn from the kitchen, where Mom made a snack. He tasted a warm bite. Then he pointed at the owl. "Read that part again," he said.

activity: common daily routines such as eating, sleeping, bathing and getting dressed
story:
Ibrahim woke up in the morning. He ate his bread and egg. Then Mama said, "Teeth time, one, two, three!" Ibrahim brushed his teeth up and down. "Good teeth," said Mama, and she smiled.

At night, Ibrahim had his bath. The water was warm. Mama helped him wash his hair. Then he put on his soft pajamas. He did not rip them. He was careful. Papa lit a small fire in the big lamp. No, wait, Papa turned on the lamp. The room felt warm and cozy. Ibrahim got into bed. Mama pulled the blanket up. "One, two, three, sleep," she said.

Then Ibrahim sat up. "Wait," he said. "My teeth!" He hopped out of bed. He ran to the bathroom. He brushed his teeth, up and down. "Good boy," said Papa. Ibrahim got back into bed. He closed his eyes. "Teeth in the morning," he said. "Teeth at night." Then he went to sleep.

story:
Edouard wanted to count all his blocks. He sat on the playroom floor. "One, two, three," he said. He stacked the blocks up high. "Four, five, six." The tower was getting tall!

He found more blocks under the chair. Dirt was on one block. He wiped the dirt off with his sleeve. "Seven, eight, nine." Only one more block to find! He looked in the toy box. He looked behind the bear. There it was, sitting all alone in the corner.

"Ten!" Edouard shouted. He had ten blocks! He wanted to write the number ten on his paper. He drew a nine first. Then he rubbed it out. Ten did not look like that. He tried again, slow and careful. He wrote a one, and then a zero. "One, zero," he read out loud. Ten needed two numbers! He held up his paper and jumped. "Mama, look! Ten!"

activity: learning to swim at the local pool
story:
Nathan stood at the little pool by the lake. The water was blue and warm. He wanted to jump in right away.

"Not yet," said his friend Daisy. "Look. There is no teacher here."

Nathan looked around. He saw the empty pool. He saw the big lake. He saw cows in the green field. The cows did not swim. They just stood in the shade.

Then Nathan saw a duck. The duck sat in the shallow water. It flapped its wings. It liked to bathe there in the sun.

"My turn soon," Nathan whispered to the duck.

At last Miss Lily came. She carried a big red float. She sat down by the pool. "Now I am watching you," she said. "You can get in."

Nathan held the red float. He kicked his legs. The water went splash, splash. His feet came up. He was floating!

"I did it!" he said. Miss Lily clapped. Nathan felt happy and warm. The duck splashed its wings too, and Nathan laughed and laughed.

activity: to count a group of up to ten objects and say which of two groups has more
story:
Oliver sat at the kitchen table. Grandma put down two rows of buttons. One row was long and spread out. One row was bunched up close.

"That long row has more!" Oliver said. "It goes all the way to the honey pot!"

"Let's count," said Grandma.

Oliver touched each button. "One, two, three, four, five." The long row had five.

Then he pushed the close row together. He counted again. "One, two, three, four, five." That row had five too.

"Same!" Oliver said. He laughed out loud.

He spread the bunched row apart. It looked big now. He pushed it back. It looked small. He counted again. Five. Five. Five.

Then Grandma slid a soft toy bee across the table. "Count these," she said.

Oliver counted fast. "Six bees, four buttons. Bees have more!"

He clapped his hands and counted them all again, just to hear the numbers go.

activity: to say a family blessing or greeting before a shared meal
story:
Emmett sat at the kitchen table. Mama set down a big pot of soup. Papa put out four orange bowls. Baby sister Ada banged her spoon.

"Can I do the special words?" Emmett asked. "Like Coco does?"

Papa smiled. "You mean bon appétit? In France, people say it before a meal. It means have a good meal."

Emmett wanted to say it too. He tried. "Bon... bon apple tea?"

Ada laughed and clapped. Mama laughed too, softly.

"Try again," said Papa. "Bon. Ap. Pé. Tit."

Emmett counted on his fingers. One, two, three, four sounds. "Bon. Ap. Pé. Tit."

"Bon appétit!" said Papa.

"Bon appétit!" said Mama.

"Ba!" said Ada, waving her spoon.

Emmett said it one more time, all by himself. Then Mama ladled soup into his orange bowl. Papa gave Ada a soft piece of bread. Emmett picked up his spoon like a big boy.

"Bon appétit, Ada," he said.

Ada blew him a kiss through the steam.

activity: to turn on a tablet, open a drawing app and put it away when done
story:
Zachary wanted to draw a big red truck. The tablet sat on the shelf, all dark and quiet. He pressed the round button at the bottom. The screen lit up, bright as morning. His mom had shown him how once, and now he could do it himself.

He tapped the little paint pot. The drawing app opened. He picked red and drew two round wheels. He drew a long truck body. He drew a driver with a funny hat.

Then the screen went black. All his truck was gone. "Where did my truck go?" he asked. Mom came over and looked. "It got tired," she said. "It needs charging." She took the charger and plugged it in for him. A small green light came on. Zachary watched from the couch and drank his juice slowly. He did not forget his truck. He waited.

After snack, the screen woke up. There was his truck, just as red as before. Zachary laughed out loud. He drew a fast dog running next to the truck. Then he was done. He pressed the button again, and the screen went dark and quiet. He carried the tablet back to the shelf with both hands.

"That was fast," said Mom. "You put it away all by yourself." Zachary patted the shelf. "Night night, tablet," he said.

activity: going on a family trip away from home
story:
Mila was going on a trip with Mama and Papa. Her teddy bear, Boo, rode in her backpack. They were off to a campsite with trees and a little tent.

First they had to fly on a big plane. At the airport, Mama put the bags on a moving belt. The belt carried Mila's backpack into a machine. The backpack went in, but it did not come out. "Boo!" said Mila. "Where is Boo?" Her tummy felt tight.

Mila stood on her toes and watched the machine. The belt moved and moved. Then, out came her backpack, on the other end. Mila opened the zipper. Boo was still there, soft and warm. "Boo came out!" said Mila. She hugged him tight. The man at the desk smiled at her. Mila felt proud. She put Boo back in the backpack and held it close.

At the campsite, the tent went up under the stars. Mila put Boo inside, safe and snug. "Night night, Boo," she said. "You rode the machine. You came back to me."

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
story:
Joshua sat in the music classroom. He wanted to play a big growly bear. His teacher, Miss Amy, stood near him. "Try the piano," she said.

Joshua pressed a key on the right. It made a high sound. That was not a bear. That was more like a little bird. He pressed a key on the far right. Another high sound. Still not a bear.

Joshua scooted down the bench. He pressed a key on the left. It made a low sound. He pressed the far left key. It made a very low sound. "Growl," said Joshua. Miss Amy laughed. "That is a big bear," she said.

Then Joshua played the high keys again. "Tweet, tweet," he sang. Miss Amy clapped. A car honked outside. Joshua stopped and smiled. He played one low key, soft and slow. "Good night, bear," he said.

activity: searching for a lost favorite toy
story:
Charles was sleepy. He rode the bus with Grandma. He hugged his blue string. His toy bunny was gone.

"Where is Bunny?" Charles asked. He looked down. The bus seat was dark under there. He could not see anything at all.

The bus driver stopped the bus. She had a little flashlight. "Try this," she said. Grandma helped Charles hold it. The light made a bright circle. Now Charles could see under the seat! There was Bunny, hiding in the dark.

"My Bunny!" said Charles. He did not throw his string. He put it in his pocket, safe. He hugged Bunny tight.

The driver smiled at him. "Good thing the light found him," she said. Charles gave Bunny a kiss on his soft ear. The bus went bump, bump, down the road. Bunny's ears went up and down. Charles laughed. He waved his string at Bunny. Bunny rode home all the way in Charles's warm arms.

activity: making an art or craft project
story:
Nova sat at the craft table at summer camp. She was drawing a picture of a snowman. She drew one ball, two balls, three balls. "Snow!" she said. "Snow in my picture."

Then Nova drew the snow. She pressed her pencil down very hard. She wanted the snow to look very white and very full. SNAP! The pencil point broke off. It rolled under the table.

"My pencil!" said Nova. "Oh no."

Her friend Ben laughed, kind and soft. "Your pencil got tired," he said. "It went to sleep."

Nova got a new pencil from the teacher. This time she pressed gently. The pencil did not snap. The snow came out soft and gray and pretty.

"One ball, two balls, three balls," said Ben.

"And one snowman," said Nova. She held up her old toy bunny. "He is in the snow too."

Ben drew a tiny carrot for the snowman's nose.

activity: to put on a coat and zip it up by themselves
story:
Sofia and Mama went to the bank. It was cold outside. "Time for your coat," said Mama. Sofia held her coat up high. She put one arm in. She put the other arm in. Now came the hard part. The zipper.

Sofia pulled the zipper tab up. It did not move. She pulled again. Still nothing. Why would it not go? She looked down at the coat. The two sides were apart at the bottom. Little bits of paper seemed to float in the air near the big machine. That was funny. But her zipper was not funny.

She looked very closely. One side of the zipper had a tiny box at the bottom. The other side had a little end. What if the end went into the box? She slid the end in. Click. It fit! Then she pulled the tab. Up it went, all the way!

"My zipper is not weak anymore," Sofia said. "It is strong!" Mama smiled. They walked out into the cold. Snow began to fall. Sofia patted her coat. "I did it all by myself," she said.

activity: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
story:
Luca lived on a farm with his grandma. One sunny morning, grandma gave him three little seeds. "Plant them here," she said. Luca dug a small hole. He put in one seed, two seeds, three seeds. Then he patted the soil down, pat, pat, pat.

Every day Luca went to look. "Where are my seeds?" he asked. Grandma said, "Wait, little one. They need rain and sun." So Luca waited. The rain came. The sun came. A naughty goat came too, but grandma shooed him away before he could nibble anything.

On the sixth day, Luca ran to the garden spot. Something green was poking up out of the soil. It was very small and very new. "Grandma, come quick!" Luca called. He ran across the yard. "A little green thing came up!"

Grandma knelt down beside him. "That is a sprout," she said. Luca looked at it. "A sprout," he said. "One sprout, two sprouts, three sprouts!" He counted them with his finger, one, two, three.

Luca made a picture of his sprouts. He drew the brown soil and the green tops. Then he showed it to the ducks by the pond. The ducks were busy watching grandpa fish in the water. Luca held up his picture anyway. "Look," he said. "My sprouts are growing."

story:
Amira sat at the big table at math club. In front of her was a red bucket full of buttons. Her friend Leo had a blue bucket.

"Want to see who has more?" asked Leo.

"Yes!" said Amira.

She grabbed some buttons from her bucket. She put them in a row. "One, two, three, four," she counted. Leo lined his up too. "One, two, three," he counted.

Amira looked at both rows. Her row was longer. "I have more!" she said. Then she wondered, what if Leo had one more?

Miss Dana came by with a little cup of buttons. Leo picked one button and put it at the end of his row.

"Count again," said Miss Dana.

"One, two, three, four," said Leo.

Now the rows were the same size. Amira tapped her chin. Hmm. Leo got one more, and now they had the same.

Miss Dana held out one button to Amira. "Here, Amira. One more for you."

Amira put it at the end of her row. She counted slowly, touching each one. "One, two, three, four, five." She jumped up. "Now I have more again!"

Leo laughed. "I want one more too!"

"Okay," said Amira. "I hope there are enough buttons."

activity: polite and functional phrases such as please, thank you, sorry and asking for help
story:
Rowan ran to the playground in his blue shirt. The sun was warm. The slide was shiny. He counted the swings. One, two, three. Then he saw a big red kite in the sky. It danced and pulled. A girl named Mia held the string. Rowan wanted to hold it so much.

He ran fast and grabbed at the string. Mia pulled it back. "No," she said. Rowan felt scared and hot in his face. His friend Sam came over. Sam said, "You say may I first." Rowan looked at the kite. He took a breath. "May I have a turn, please?" he asked.

Mia smiled. "Yes, you may," she said. She put the string in his hand. The kite pulled like a big dog. Rowan laughed. "Thank you, Mia," he said. Then he tripped on the grass and tumbled down. "Sorry, kite," he said, and Sam helped him up. "Thank you," Rowan said again.

They took turns, one, two, three, four. The wind went whoosh. The kite went up and up. "May I fly it now?" asked Sam. "Yes, you may," said Rowan. He held the string tight and watched the red tail wave.

story:
Mohamed sat in his car seat. The car went bump, bump over the road. "Where are we going?" he asked. "To Grandma's house," said Mama. "She is making soup." Mohamed watched the trees go by. The sun made his seat warm. "Hot," he said, and pulled his hand away. The window was cool when Mama opened it a little. Warm seat, cool wind. The same car had two different feelings.

At Grandma's house, the big pot sat on the stove. Grandma stirred it with a long spoon. Mohamed looked at the stove. It did not look like anything at all. Was it hot? Was it cold? He could not tell. He put his hands behind his back. "Grandma, is the stove hot?" he asked. Grandma held her hand up high, far from the pot. "Yes, it is still hot," she said. "Only I touch the stove. You can watch from here." Mohamed stood by the door, close to Mama. The soup went bubble, bubble.

Later the pot was empty. Everyone ate the soup. It was warm and good. In the car going home, Mohamed felt sleepy. "Talk about it tomorrow," said Mama softly. Mohamed had a dream about bubbles, big and round, going up, up, up.

story:

Next, Weston wanted the red cup. It was too far away. He stretched and stretched. His chair wobbled like a little storm at sea. "Help, please," said Weston. Papa reached over and gave him the red cup. Weston took a big drink. "Ahh," he said. "Yummy water."

Then Grandma came in the door. Weston hid behind his hands. Grandma waved at him. Weston peeked out. "Hello," he said. Grandma clapped her hands. She gave him a tiny orange from her pocket, like a little sun. Weston held it up to the light. "Hello, orange," he whispered, and he took a great big bite of his rice.

story:
Snow fell outside the window. Kinsley wanted to watch it fall. She pushed the couch to see better. Behind the couch, she saw a small hole in the wall. It had two little slots. It looked like a tiny face.

Kinsley wanted to touch it. She lifted her finger. Then she remembered. Fingers never go in there. She put her hand behind her back. She ran to find Grandma.

"Grandma, come see," said Kinsley. "There is a hole behind the couch." Grandma came right away. She looked at the wall. "That is an outlet," said Grandma. "Thank you for telling me, not touching it." Grandma put a safe cover on it. It clicked into place.

"Now it is closed," said Grandma. Kinsley touched the cover. It felt smooth and cool. The cover did not open for her finger. It stayed shut.

Grandma gave her paper and paint. Kinsley painted white snow. She painted the couch. She painted the outlet with its new cover, and it looked just like the true thing. Then she held Grandma's hand, and together they watched the snow.

story:
Wesley wanted to play a game. Daddy put three things on the bath mat. "Close your eyes," said Daddy. Wesley shut his eyes tight.

First he touched a stone. His fingertips slid round and round. It felt smooth. "A stone!" said Wesley. He opened his eyes. Yes, it was a stone.

Next his fingertips found bumps. Bumpy all over. "The pinecone!" He was right again.

Then something soft tickled his fingers. It felt like a little feather. Wesley laughed. "The feather!" Daddy clapped.

Daddy held up a toothbrush. Wesley saw its straight handle. He heard the tap run. The toothpaste smelled like mint. He put a little on his tongue. It tasted cool. Then he chewed his breakfast dream away and brushed every tooth. Daddy said, "All clean, big boy." Wesley smiled at himself in the mirror.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
story:
Paisley wanted a story at bedtime. She ran to her shelf. But the book felt wrong. It was not her book.

Dad came in. "Where did my book go?" Paisley asked. "The one with the funny dog."

"Maybe you left it at school," said Dad. "But here is a library book. We can read this one."

Paisley looked at the cover. There were little marks on it. "What are these?" she asked. Dad pointed. "Those are words. That name says Eric. He made up the story."

Paisley touched the name with her finger. "Eric made the dog?" she asked.

"This Eric made this book," said Dad. "Your book has a name too."

Dad opened the book at the back. Paisley shook her head. She turned the pages herself. She turned them until she got to the front. The first page had a picture.

"Start here," she said.

So Dad read, and Paisley listened, and the pages turned one by one to the end.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: getting a first library card and borrowing a book
story:
Zayn put on his red shoe. "I need the other one," he said. Mom laughed and found it under the couch.

At the library, a lady gave Zayn a little card. It had his name on it. "My own card!" said Zayn. He picked a book about a big, juicy strawberry. The lady scanned the card. Zayn hugged the book all the way home.

Daddy read the book three times. Then Zayn took it back to the library. He slid it into the return slot. The book went down, down, gone. "Bye, book," said Zayn. Then he looked for his shelf. He wanted a new book about trucks. He held it up. The lady smiled. "Your card again?" she asked. Zayn gave her the same little card. It worked! Zayn jumped. "It's a magic card," he said. "Not magic," said Mom, "but pretty great." Zayn hugged the truck book tight.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: learning to swim at the local pool
story:
Miles stood in the pool changing room. He put on his little blue swimsuit. "Time for swim class," said Dad. Miles held his yellow owl towel. "Can the owl swim too?" asked Miles. "No, but he can watch," said Dad.

At the pool, Miles wanted to get out. He pulled on the wet edge. His arms slipped. His feet splashed. He could not get out. "This is hard," said Miles. His teacher pointed to the metal ladder. Miles put his feet on the ladder steps. Up, up, up he went. "I did it!" said Miles.

He slid back into the water. Then he climbed the ladder again. "Is the ladder easy?" asked Dad. "Yes!" said Miles. "The ladder helps me!" He hugged his owl towel. "Good tries, Miles," said Dad. Miles smiled big.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: starting the first day of school
story:
David climbed the tall steps of the school bus. He found a seat by the window. His backpack sat on his lap. Today was his first day of school!

The bus went bump, bump, bump. David saw a dog out the window. He saw a red truck. Soon the bus stopped at school. A big door waited at the top of the steps.

Inside, David saw blocks and paint and a tiny play kitchen. His teacher smiled and said, "Good morning, David!" Then David needed to go to the bathroom. He looked around. He could not find it. Where was it? He asked himself, "Who can help me?"

He walked to his teacher. "I need to find the bathroom," he said. "I will show you," she said. She took his hand. They walked down the hall. The bathroom was right there! David washed his hands all by himself.

At play time, David built a tall tower of blocks. A girl named Mia knocked it over by accident. "It's okay," said David. "I can ask the teacher if I need help." After snack, David drew a picture of the school bus. He could not reach the red crayon. Mia got it for him. Then the teacher rang a bell. "Time for the bus!" she said.

David ran to the bus with his class. He waved at his teacher. "See you tomorrow!" he called. The bus went bump, bump, bump all the way home.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
story:
Everett sat in a big chair at the doctor's office. He wanted a sticker, but first he had to wait. The wait felt long. He looked around with his eyes. He saw a man with a bandage on his arm. He heard a phone ring with his ears. He smelled something like soap with his nose.

Then the nurse came in. "Time to check you," she said. She let Everett touch the paper on the bed. The paper was smooth and it made a crinkly sound. Everett touched it with his fingers. The nurse smiled. "Good looking, good listening," she said.

Next she held up a little cup. "This is lemon juice," she said. "You can try a tiny taste with your tongue." Everett thought of orange juice. Orange juice was sweet. So lemon juice must be sweet too. He stuck out his tongue and tasted it. He scrunched up his whole face. "Sour!" he said. "Sour, sour!" The nurse laughed, and the man in the hall laughed too.

Everett got his sticker at last. It was a shiny star. He stuck it on his hand and looked at it with his eyes. "Sour lemon," he told his mom. "Sour lemon, sweet sticker."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: polite and functional phrases such as please, thank you, sorry and asking for help
story:
Madelyn wanted apple juice. She sat at the table. Her cup was empty.

"Give me juice!" said Madelyn.

Daddy kept cutting the apple. He did not bring the juice. Madelyn tried again.

"Juice, please," said Madelyn.

Daddy smiled. "Juice coming up!" He poured the juice into her cup. Madelyn took a big drink. "Thank you," she said. "You are welcome," said Daddy.

Then Madelyn tipped her cup. The juice spilled on the floor. "Oh no," said Madelyn. "Sorry, Daddy."

"That is okay," said Daddy. "Please get the towel." Madelyn ran to the drawer. She got the small towel. She wiped the floor all by herself.

Then Madelyn wanted to feed the dog. "Please come here," she called. The dog ran over. It began to bark. "Thank you," said Madelyn, and she put food in the bowl.

After lunch, Madelyn felt sleepy. The dog was already asleep by the door. Daddy carried Madelyn to her bed. "Can you read to me, please?" she asked.

"Yes," said Daddy. He opened the book. Outside, a butterfly flew past the window. Madelyn watched it until her eyes closed.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: welcoming a new baby brother or sister into the family
story:
Mia ran into the baby store. "The baby is coming soon!" she said. Mom smiled. "We need a little bed," she said. Outside it was windy, but inside the store was warm. Mia liked the tiny socks. She held one up. It was smaller than her thumb.

Then Mia saw a doll. It had a soft head. She picked it up. The doll's head flopped down. It flopped to the side. Mia gasped. "Oh no!" she said. She held the doll again. This time she put her hand under its head. The head stayed still. "I have an idea," said Mia. "I will hold the baby like this."

A lady walked by with a real baby. She had her hand under the baby's head. Mia watched. The baby's head did not flop. "Just like my doll!" said Mia. Mom picked out a little blanket. It had white snow dots all over it. Mia carried the blanket to the car, and the doll rode home with her hand under its head.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: recovering from a cold or flu at home
story:
Victoria sat at the table. She had oatmeal and a banana. The sky outside was cloudy. Victoria sniffed. She sniffed again. Then she sniffed a third time.

"My nose is drippy," said Victoria. She wiped it on her sleeve. Mom brought a box of tissues. Mom pulled one tissue out. "Try this," said Mom. Victoria held the soft tissue. She blew her nose. One big sniff, and the tissue did the work. "My nose feels better now," said Victoria. She hoped the drips were all gone. She looked out at the big tree.

"I need a tissue," said Victoria next time. She took one, then two, then three tissues. She made a little pile. "One for me. One for Bear. One for Bunny," she said. Mom smiled and gave Bear a pat.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to clap along to the steady beat of a song and sing a nursery rhyme from memory
story:
Edouard stood in the music room. A drum sat in front of Miss Pia. "Today we clap," she said. She tapped the drum. Boom, boom, boom.

Edouard clapped too fast. His claps ran ahead of the drum. "Too quick, Edouard!" said his friend Tom. Tom laughed, but not in a mean way. Edouard clapped too slow. His claps fell behind. He frowned.

Then Miss Pia sang a little song. "Twinkle, twinkle, little star." The words were short. The ends of the lines matched. Star, star, are, high. Edouard clapped with the song. Boom went his hands. One clap for each beat. His claps fit!

"Can I sing it by myself?" he asked Tom. "Try it," said Tom. Edouard sang the whole song. He did not forget one word. He clapped all the way too. Miss Pia played a long drum roll. "Our star!" she said. Edouard took a bow, just like a big singer, and Tom clapped for him this time.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: welcoming a new baby brother or sister into the family
story:
Alexander went to the baby store with Mama. "The new baby needs things," said Mama. Alexander wanted to pick a toy. He found a red cup with a duck on it. "The baby can drink from this!" he said. He also found a shiny pinwheel. "The baby can watch it spin!" Mama smiled. "Babies sleep a lot," she said. "Maybe the baby will sleep now."

At home, the baby came. Alexander held the pinwheel up. "Look! Spin!" he said. But the baby was sleeping again. Alexander waited. He blew the pinwheel softly. Still the baby slept. "Does the baby sleep all day?" he whispered. He spun the cup round and round on the table. It made a little sound. The baby opened one eye.

Then the baby made a small noise. "He is awake!" said Alexander. Mama put the baby in her arms. Alexander touched the baby's tiny hand. The baby held on. Alexander laughed. "Now we can play," he said. "But just a little bit." The pinwheel sat on the shelf, waiting for tomorrow.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: basic shape concepts such as circle, square, triangle and rectangle
story:
Ava sat at the art table. She had a small pile of stickers. She wanted to put a sticker on her toy block.

The block had lost its color in one spot. Ava wanted to fix it.

She put one sticker on the top. It was a square sticker on a square face. Then she put one on the bottom. She turned the block over and over.

"Look, Ava," said Teacher Mia. She held the block up. She did not say more.

Ava counted the stickers. "One, two, three, four, five, six." The block had six faces. Each face was a square. Six square faces, six square stickers!

Then Ava saw something else. Her friend Sam had a round ball. Ava pressed a sticker on it. The sticker peeled off. It would not stay on the curved skin of the ball. A square sticker likes a flat face.

Ava laughed. "The ball will not take my sticker," she said.

Teacher Mia smiled. "You can give the ball round stickers instead."

Ava took out a circle sticker, a triangle sticker, and a rectangle sticker too. She put the circle on a round lid. She put the triangle on a paper hat. She put the rectangle on a little door.

Then she set the block on the table. "Six stickers, six squares," said Ava.

Sam clapped his hands.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: playing on a sports team for the season
story:
Madison put on her red team shirt. The sun was warm on the court. Her shoes went squeak, squeak on the dry ground. "I think it will be a good day," she said.

The game started. Madison ran and bounced the ball. She threw it up. It did not go in. The other team got more baskets. The coach blew the whistle. The game was over.

The other team jumped and smiled. Madison felt mad. She wanted to stomp her foot. "Do we have to keep playing?" she asked. "No," said Coach Amy. "Now we line up."

Madison stood in the line. Each player on her team gave a high five. Each player on the other team said, "Good game." Then it was Madison's turn. She heard herself say it too. "Good game."

The girl in the blue shirt smiled at her. "Your bounce pass was nice," the girl said. Madison stood taller. She looked up at the sky. The weather was still warm. She waved to the blue team as they walked away.
